record.paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Security and privacy for causal explanations
record.original_question: How can explanation systems that use causal knowledge, such as feature attribution, causal Shapley values, or causal recourse, be protected from attacks that exploit predictions and explanations to extract decision boundaries, infer membership in training data, or recover the causal graph or explanation model?

evidence.quote: Consider a deployed ML system that provides explanations to its users, e.g., through access to an API. In such settings, an adversary may combine predictions and explanations to extract an approximate model as well as information about the data used to train it.

In the case of models using causal knowledge about the DGP (Secs. 5.1.3, 5.1.4 and 5.2.2), we hypothesize that it is important to guard this causal knowledge against causal-discovery-like model extraction attacks too.
There has been very limited work on guarding explanation methods against such concerns.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a machine learning system deployed behind a query interface that, for each input x in an input space X, returns both a prediction f(x) and a causal explanation E(x). The explanation map E may take one of the following forms:

(a) a feature attribution vector φ(x) ∈ R^d assigning importance scores to the d input features;
(b) causal Shapley values, computed with respect to a structural causal model M = (G, F, P) consisting of a directed acyclic graph G over variables {X_1,…,X_d}, structural assignments F, and a noise distribution P, such that the attribution to feature i accounts for causal effects along directed paths in G;
(c) causal recourse, returning, for an individual x with unfavorable prediction, a minimum-cost intervention do(X_S = x_S') (S ⊆ {1,…,d}) under M that flips the prediction.

An adversary has black-box query access to the pair (f, E) and may submit an adaptively chosen sequence of queries x^(1), x^(2), … ∈ X, observing (f(x^(k)), E(x^(k))) for each. Define the following three adversarial objectives:

1. Model extraction: produce a surrogate f̂ : X → Y minimizing Pr_{x∼D}[f̂(x) ≠ f(x)] for some data distribution D.
2. Membership inference: given a candidate point z, decide whether z belongs to the training set used to fit f and M.
3. Causal-structure extraction: recover the underlying causal graph G (or the structural assignments F, or the explanation model itself) up to Markov equivalence or some stronger criterion.

Design defense mechanisms (e.g., randomized explanations, query auditing, differential-privacy–style noise mechanisms, or restrictions on E) D acting on (f, E) such that, for every polynomial-time adversary issuing at most N queries, each of the above three adversarial objectives can be provably bounded — for instance, ε-differential privacy of the released explanations with respect to the training data, an (N, ε)-bound on agreement of any surrogate f̂ with f, and an (N, δ)-bound on the probability of recovering G — while simultaneously preserving a prescribed level of fidelity of the explanations E to the true causal effects induced by M. Determine whether such mechanisms exist, characterize the achievable trade-offs between utility (explanation fidelity) and security (the above bounds), and exhibit concrete constructions.
artifact.status_search_result: This is posed as an open research direction: while model-extraction and membership-inference attacks against standard explanation methods (e.g., LIME, SHAP) have been studied, defenses tailored to causal explanations (causal Shapley values, causal recourse) and protection of the underlying causal graph against causal-discovery-style extraction remain largely unaddressed in the literature, and no general solution with provable utility–security trade-offs is known.

status_evidence.claim: The problem of defending causal explanation systems against extraction, membership, and causal-structure recovery attacks is identified as open.
